questions.question: Q: What is the AIDA model and how do advertisers use it?
questions.correctAnswer: AIDA stands for Attention (grab the audience with a striking image or headline), Interest (hold attention with engaging content), Desire (make the audience want the product by showing benefits), and Action (tell them what to do — 'buy now', 'visit our website'). Most adverts follow this structure to move audiences from awareness to purchase.

questions.question: Q: How has digital technology changed advertising?
questions.correctAnswer: Digital technology has enabled: personalised behavioural targeting using data tracking, programmatic advertising (automated buying), social media and influencer marketing, interactive and video ads, native advertising that blends with content, and real-time performance measurement. This makes advertising more targeted but raises privacy concerns.

questions.question: Q: Evaluate the regulation of advertising in the UK.
questions.correctAnswer: The ASA provides independent regulation, requiring adverts to be legal, decent, honest, and truthful. This protects consumers from misleading claims and harmful content. However, regulation struggles to keep pace with digital advertising — influencer marketing, native advertising, and online targeting often fall outside traditional rules. questions.question: Full-Mark Response Analyse how one of your advertising CSPs targets and appeals to its audience. [15 marks] <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Advertising uses a range of media language techniques to target and appeal to specific audiences, guided by the AIDA model and informed by detailed audience profiling. The visual codes of the advert are designed to attract the target audience's attention. The choice of imagery — whether featuring aspirational lifestyles, relatable people, or striking visuals — is determined by psychographic profiling. For example, adverts targeting 'aspirers' (psychographic group) use images of success, luxury, and social status to create desire. The written codes reinforce the visual message. Headlines use direct address ('You deserve this') to create personal connection, while body copy emphasises benefits over features. Slogans create memorable brand associations through repetition and linguistic devices (alliteration, rhyme, puns). Celebrity endorsement leverages the star's cultural meaning (Dyer's star theory) to transfer positive associations to the product. The celebrity's star image — carefully constructed through media appearances — carries connotations that the brand wishes to associate with. The mode of address is crucial: informal, direct language targets younger audiences; sophisticated, understated language targets affluent audiences. This demonstrates how language choices are determined by audience profiling. Digital targeting has refined this further.
